definition: Iconoclast means one who attacks established beliefs and institutions.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word iconoclast. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know iconoclast should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The food critic made her name as an iconoclast, arguing in print that the city's most beloved steakhouse had been coasting on its legend for forty years.
A critic finds fault and says so; that alone is far short of an iconoclast.
A dissenter goes further than a critic, refusing the majority view outright, but stops short of an iconoclast, who swings at the revered institution itself.

A rebel fights authority — the rules, the boss, the government — often simply to resist being told what to do. An iconoclast picks a different target: not the people in charge but the things everyone reveres, the sacred models and beloved traditions. A rebel breaks rules; an iconoclast breaks idols.

A skeptic doubts: shown a revered theory, a skeptic withholds belief and asks for better evidence. An iconoclast goes on the attack, working to tear the revered thing down in public. Skepticism is a quiet habit of mind; an iconoclast swings a hammer where a skeptic only raises an eyebrow.

Iconoclast means one who attacks established beliefs and institutions.

Every September the economics faculty assigns its freshmen the same revered growth model, and every September Professor Aldana opens his first lecture by attacking it — the assumptions, the data behind it, even the fame of the man who built it.
He is the department's iconoclast, and he grades hardest the essays that agree with him too easily.

Iconoclast is Greek for 'image-breaker,' and it is stronger than 'rebel': a rebel resists being told what to do, while an iconoclast turns and attacks what everyone else reveres — the sacred model, the founding legend, the untouchable rule.
The word keeps its edge of demolition.
Reach for iconoclast when someone does not just leave the beaten path but attacks the path itself — the revered model, the sacred tradition.
A maverick (also in this unit) merely refuses to run with the herd, and heterodox describes the contrary opinions rather than the person swinging them.
Iconoclast always carries the sound of something breaking.

For thirty years Professor Ada Quist has made a career of swinging at monuments.
Her first book argued that the beloved national epic was a patchwork of borrowings; her second called the country's most revered painter a gifted copyist.
Quist obeys every university rule, sits on committees without complaint, and has never once picketed an administration building.
It is not authority she attacks but reverence itself — an iconoclast, colleagues sigh, is hardest on whatever the rest of us kneel to.
Asked why, she answers that a tradition worth keeping should be able to survive a hammer blow or two.
